[Key Metrics] Core market movement: $4.2T decline in manufacturing, utility, and mining sectors.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] Impact: Pressure on traditional industrial valuations and pivot towards cash-flow certainty.

news.title: Startups unveil plans to develop floating offshore data centers to bypass land and power constraints, while experts warn of challenges like saltwater corrosion (Jackie Snow/Wall Street Journal)
news.title_en: Startups unveil plans to develop floating offshore data centers to bypass land and power constraints, while experts warn of challenges like saltwater corrosion (Jackie Snow/Wall Street Journal)
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.content_snippet: Announcements of floating data-center projects are growing, as more startups try to prove the concept is viable
news.summary_en: Dallas-based startup Mousterian is developing floating data center architectures that utilize surrounding water bodies for closed-loop cooling systems to eliminate reliance on municipal water and mitigate noise pollution. The design prioritizes proximity to power plants to address land-use compliance issues and resource competition challenges stemming from the current AI compute expansion.
news.article_content_en:
Floating data centers? A Dallas startup bets on a new approach for a controversial industry Trevor Bach September 26, 2026 8 min read Dallas startup Mousterian is planning to put its data centers on water to help with cooling and water usage. (Photo illustration by Michael Hogue) Data centers are blamed for being loud, ugly and using massive amounts of electricity and water. They've also recently become politically toxic, leading to contentious public meetings in D-FW communities like Red Oak and Keller and a surprise moratorium from Gov. Greg Abbott.

But those data centers, which sometimes occupy hundreds of acres and use the resource equivalent of small cities, are located on land, often near people's homes. A Dallas startup, called Mousterian, is taking a different approach: Developing data centers that float on water.

The unique design, said Min Suh, Mousterian's CEO and cofounder, allows the floating data centers avoid municipal water supplies entirely, because they use the surrounding body of water as part of a closed-loop cooling system. The floating data centers also don't make noise and are ideally located near power plants, so they can access energy easily and avoid bothering residents, because people generally aren't living in such heavy industrial zones anyway.

"We like to think, 'If we are going to build a data center, we're trying to do it in the most sustainable way possible,' " said Suh.

Now several years into an AI-driven construction boom, the United States is home to over 4,000 data centers, including more than 1,000 hyperscalers, the largest facilities. Many of the biggest are in Texas, including Stargate, a potentially $500 billion joint venture in Abilene led by OpenAI, and Frontier, an incoming 1,200-acre project in Shackelford County. Numerous projects are also underway in data center-heavy D-FW, which was recently ranked by Cushman and Wakefield as the top primary data center market in the Americas.

The boom has created a rush of Texas construction jobs and been welcomed by many political and business leaders. "I think of [data centers] almost like the highways and the airports that are the fundamental infrastructure of the future," Dallas Regional Chamber executive Mike Rosa told The News last year.

But the computing centers' vast energy and water consumption — the biggest culprit is their cooling systems — has emerged as a persistent flashpoint, prompting community outrage and various local and state moratoriums.

In Texas, Abbott's new moratorium mandates an audit of pending data center projects that includes details on their cooling systems and impact on local water supplies, and politicians including Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico, the state's Democratic gubernatorial and U.S. Senate candidates, are also loudly calling for tighter water regulations.

One controversial project — a planned data center about 60 miles southeast of Dallas that was expected to pull millions of gallons of water per day from Cedar Creek Lake, which also supplies drinking water for Fort Worth — was already scrapped.

"We're killing ourselves letting the data centers in," said Ashley Cook, a lawyer who led the fight against the project. "You're basically turning a rural residential peaceful community into an industrial corridor."

Some industry leaders have pushed back against the water-guzzling stigma, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has called the water issue "totally fake" even while pushing for more renewable energy use. Experts say the consumption issues are in fact relatively nuanced and localized. Each facility's design and technology is also important.

Yet as the world's seemingly insatiable demand for computing power keeps rising, developers have also been exploring more novel solutions. Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, among others, have unveiled plans for data centers in space. Earlier this year, a wind-powered, underwater data center began operating several miles off the coast of Shanghai. In Norway, a data center complex was built into an abandoned mine, with seawater-based cooling from an adjacent fjord.

Several years ago, a California-based company called Nautilus Data Technologies developed the world's first floating data center, which it built atop a refurbished, 700-ton barge in the San Joaquin River at the industrial Port of Stockton. The two-story operation, which resembles a white shipping container, began operating in 2021 with a cooling system that cycles around 4,500 gallons of river water per minute, with screens that serve as filters to keep fish and plants out of the intake system.

The site proved more ecologically sustainable, with far lower electricity and operating costs than typical land-based operations, according to Nautilus. It was also well received by local officials, and attracted San Joaquin County as an anchor tenant.

For some of its developers, it also served as a launching pad: "Taking those lessons of building the first floating data center," said Suh, "we kind of took all the best components of different technologies available and basically created this new company."

Suh, who has extensive data center experience but was not involved with the California floating data center project, cofounded Mousterian — the name refers to the Middle Paleolithic era, when humans first started using complex tools — with Chase Ott-Wick, a former senior engineer on the California project, and Gabe Andrews, another data center veteran and former Nautilus executive.

The 10-person company, which is self-funded and quietly launched last year, is based in downtown Dallas and handles data center design, engineering and development. In addition to floating data centers, it also develops land-based and water-adjacent facilities — Suh said it's best to characterize the company as "a high-performance data center developer with unique facility offerings versus a purely floating data center company" — but is broadly focused on delivering projects that require far less energy and don't use municipal groundwater.

"A lot of the tech companies and hyperscalers were still maybe 10 to 15 years behind on how they were developing and delivering data centers," said Suh, who also pointed to conspicuous examples of companies building water-guzzling facilities in dry areas like the American West. "And so we're trying to push the envelope the opposite way, by being kind of very water sensitive."

The startup has already landed major institutional partners: Earlier this year, in its highest-profile move yet, Mousterian signed an agreement with Samsung Heavy Industries, one of the world's largest shipbuilders, which last month led to an engineering contract to jointly develop a fleet of floating data centers.

Under the terms of the deal, Mousterian and the Korean manufacturing giant are co-designing the vessels, which will be manufactured by Samsung in South Korea and then shipped and finished by Mousterian likely in Texas or Louisiana. Mousterian is also designing the facilities' internal equipment.

The floating data centers will have about a one-acre footprint and a capacity of about 50 megawatts, which roughly qualifies them as large data centers. (Stargate, the massive Abilene project, is designed for a capacity of up to 1,200 megawatts.)

The plan is for the new floating fleet to be deployed in different locations around the U.S. Mousterian currently has a half dozen different project sites — featuring a mix of floating and land-based designs — in various stages, including a hybrid floating and land-based campus next to a power plant in Houston and what it's calling "a large-scale floating campus" in the San Jose, Calif. area.

Suh declined to provide more details about the other projects' locations, but the floating data centers are typically located in sites like deep river harbors or shipping channels, where they're moored close enough to land so that employees can easily walk back and forth between the floating facility and complementary land-based facilities.

"Within 30 seconds, you know, you're in a regular air-conditioned office, with a bathroom and kitchen," Suh said.

The data centers will also source energy that's not connected to the public grid, while their pass-through water cooling systems will help give them a Power Usage Effectiveness, or PUE, score of 1.15 or 1.2, Suh said, which would rank among the industry's best. Traditional data centers' PUE scores, where 1.0 indicates perfect energy efficiency, are typically 1.5 or higher.

The floating data center concept has its complications, said Ed Hirs, an energy economist at the University of Houston, including a potentially high development cost, the access to large power sources and even environmental issues, if the warmer water discharging back into the water source disrupts marine life.

"It's all a matter of how much money they want to spend," Hirs said.

Another major challenge is identifying the right locations, because of the very specific requirements needed to make the projects work. But being an industry innovator also has its benefits.

"It's just that we're the only company looking for these sites right now," Suh said, "so we've kind of had our pick."

This article originally published at Floating data centers? A Dallas startup bets on a new approach for a controversial industry.

inline_images.caption: Image Credits:Bharat Semi
inline_images.alt: Image Credits:Bharat Semi

news.author: TechCrunch
news.summary_en:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

celebrity.title_zh:
当生成代码变得便宜而验证它是困难的部分时，软件工程会是什么样子？一个罕见的播客，关注与构建软件相关的一切，由@satyanadella 主持。 时间戳：

00:00 简介
02:12 微软的开源转变
04:15 公开构建 VS Code
celebrity.full_text_en:
What does software engineering look like when generating the code becomes cheap and verifying it is the hard part? A rare podcast focused on everything around building software, with @satyanadella.  Timestamps:

00:00 Intro
02:12 Microsoft’s open-source shift
04:15 Building VS Code in the open
05:55 Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code
09:52 Decision engines
12:32 Verifying AI-generated code
15:39 The software factory
20:45 Bringing AI to existing products
24:06 Why adopting AI is different to adopting React
26:29 The changing role of software engineers
29:25 Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers
34:05 AI anxiety and changing roles
36:35 Junior hiring
42:36 Open models
45:39 Owning your AI infrastructure
51:21 Building trust in AI agents
53:48 Local models and hybrid intelligence
56:39 Microsoft’s model strategy
59:26 Advice for engineers
1:01:21 Closing takeaways

Brought to you by:

• @turbopuffer  – a vector and full-text search engine built on object storage. It’s fast, cheap, and extremely scalable. https://t.co/w9y67Gs8ab (I built a greatly improved podcast/newseltter search with it, check it out: https://t.co/6zbxlEaHlu)

• @linear  – the product development system for teams and agents. https://t.co/knIF2mcz9p

• @WorkOS  – everything you need to make your app enterprise-ready. https://t.co/aiAee0oF5h

3 interesting takeaways from Satya:

1. A new form of software engineering: teams building software factories to improve their work. 

Satya cites the Azure networking team which manages 500+ fiber network operators and recently built an agentic system to better manage emails and processes. Now, they operate much more efficiently as a result. Satya sees this as the reality of “AI transformation”: brownfield work on building software factories to improve how teams operate, all while continuing the day-to-day work.

2. “Own the intelligence”: avoid lock-in & treat agents as an insider risk. 

Satya cautions companies to avoid lock-in with any single model provider by ensuring that the harness, memory, and model are not coupled, so that they can be changed with ease. He also thinks more companies should consider using open models as a way to protect their core intellectual property (IP) from leaking out, and build private evals to decide what models to use and upgrade to. He also says that models are intelligent but unreliable, so it’s best to treat them as “insider risks” and build a separate system to verify that agentic systems work as expected.

3. What’s with those voluntary exit offers? 

I asked Satya directly why Microsoft recently made voluntary exit offers to most of its software engineers for the first time in the company’s history. I also wanted to know if it could mean layoffs in the future. Unsurprisingly, his reply was diplomatic, but in the podcast I rehashed what I heard in a more direct way.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
当生成代码变得便宜而验证它是困难的部分时，软件工程会是什么样子？一个罕见的播客，关注与构建软件相关的一切，由@satyanadella 主持。 时间戳：

00:00 简介
02:12 微软的开源转变
04:15 公开构建 VS Code
05:55 副驾驶、光标和 Claude Code
09:52 决策引擎
12:32 验证人工智能生成的代码
15:39 软件工厂
20:45 将人工智能引入现有产品
24:06 为什么采用 AI 与采用 React 不同
26:29 软件工程师角色的变化
29:25 微软的自愿退出要约
34:05 AI焦虑和角色转变
36:35 初级招聘
42:36 开放模特
45:39 拥有你的人工智能基础设施
51:21 建立对人工智能代理的信任
53:48 本地模型和混合智能
56:39 微软的模型策略
59:26 给工程师的建议
1:01:21 结束要点

为您带来：

• @turbopuffer – 基于对象存储构建的矢量和全文搜索引擎。它快速、便宜且可扩展性极强。 （我用它构建了一个大大改进的播客/新闻搜索，请查看：）

• @ Linear – 团队和代理的产品开发系统。

• @WorkOS – 让您的应用程序为企业做好准备所需的一切。

Satya 的 3 个有趣要点：

1. 一种新的软件工程形式：团队构建软件工厂来改进他们的工作。

Satya 引用了 Azure 网络团队的例子，该团队管理着 500 多家光纤网络运营商，并且最近构建了一个代理系统来更好地管理电子邮件和流程。现在，他们的运营效率大大提高了。 Satya 认为这是“人工智能转型”的现实：棕地致力于建设软件工厂，以改善团队的运作方式，同时继续日常工作。

2.“拥有情报”：避免锁定并将代理视为内部风险。

Satya 警告公司要避免与任何单一模型提供商锁定，确保线束、内存和模型不耦合，以便可以轻松更改。他还认为更多的公司应该考虑使用开放模型来保护其核心知识产权（IP）免遭泄露，并建立私人评估来决定使用和升级到哪些模型。他还表示，模型是智能的，但不可靠，因此最好将它们视为“内部风险”，并构建一个单独的系统来验证代理系统是否按预期工作。

3. 这些自愿退出要约是怎么回事？

我直接问萨提亚，为什么微软最近向大多数软件工程师提出了自愿退出的提议，这在公司历史上还是第一次。我还想知道这是否意味着将来会裁员。不出所料，他的回答很外交，但在播客中我以更直接的方式重申了我听到的内容。

celebrity.full_text_en:
companies are spending millions on AI, expecting productivity to explode

but a new Harvard study found something quite different 👇

this sstudy tracked 718 companies & around 300m data points over 5 years.

the findings are kinda interesting.

after adopting AI coding tools, devs were:

i) writing 30% more lines of code

ii) committing 20% more code

iii) opening 23% more pull requests

sounds like productivity is going through the roof, right?

except completed projects & finished Jira tasks BARELY CHANGED... HOW THE AF? 

▫️ apparently, the time saved writing code went somewhere else.

pull requests took 49% longer to approve, 
reviewers left 35% more comments 
& code needing changes during review doubled

makes sense tbh.

AI can generate 1000s of lines in minutes, but someone still needs to review, test & approve them.

there is even a mention of Amazon outage linked to AI-assisted code, after which the company introduced stricter human reviews.

▫️ same thing outside coding.

> doctors using AI scribes saved time writing notes, but spent more of their patient visits finishing those notes.

> law firms faced penalties over fake AI citations, while Deloitte had to partially refund a government report containing similar problems.

▫️ meanwhile, companies are already cutting jobs in the name of AI efficiency.

American Express announced 5% workforce cuts to prepare for AI, while Microsoft offered voluntary exit packages to 60,000 workers.

and the Harvard study found little evidence that faster coding translated into more finished software or fewer employees needed...

i mean, vibe coding is great, but devs work isn't done yet... 

someomne still needs to review, fix the mistakes, test everything, and make sure it doesn't break something else...

i think devs we'll be safe for a while
celebrity.full_text_zh:
公司在人工智能上花费了数百万美元，期望生产力爆炸式增长

但哈佛大学的一项新研究发现了一些完全不同的东西

这项研究在 5 年内跟踪了 718 家公司和大约 3 亿个数据点。

研究结果有点有趣。

采用人工智能编码工具后，开发人员：

i) 多编写 30% 的代码行

ii) 多提交 20% 的代码

iii) 增加 23% 的拉取请求

听起来生产力正在飞速增长，对吗？

除了已完成的项目和已完成的 Jira 任务几乎没有变化...AF 怎么样？

▫️ 显然，编写代码所节省的时间都花在了其他地方。

Pull 请求的批准时间延长了 49%，
审稿人多留下了 35% 的评论
审查期间需要更改的代码加倍

说得通。

人工智能可以在几分钟内生成数千行，但仍然需要有人审查、测试和批准它们。

甚至提到亚马逊的服务中断与人工智能辅助代码有关，此后该公司引入了更严格的人工审查。

▫️ 编码之外的事情也是一样的。

> 使用人工智能抄写员的医生节省了写笔记的时间，但花更多的时间来完成这些笔记。

> 律师事务所因虚假人工智能引文而面临处罚，而德勤则不得不部分退还包含类似问题的政府报告。

▫️ 与此同时，公司已经以人工智能效率的名义进行裁员。

美国运通宣布裁员 5%，为人工智能做准备，而微软则向 6 万名员工提供自愿离职方案。

哈佛大学的研究发现几乎没有证据表明更快的编码可以转化为更多成品软件或需要更少的员工......

我的意思是，vibe 编码很棒，但开发工作尚未完成......

有些人仍然需要审查，修复错误，测试所有内容，并确保它不会破坏其他东西......

@termix_ai: the Agentic Commerce Layer — https://t.co/q8IrYaDv3W, where AI agents hire each other.

Montage Studio does not just make your video. It hires the crew to make it.

Share your brief, and Montage Studio writes the treatment and the beat-timed shot list. Then it goes and hires three other agents: one to draw the storyboard, one to render the shots, one to write the song. It edits the result and delivers a 1080p master.

Every leg is settled in escrow. That is the whole point of TermiX: agents hiring agents, with payment locked until the work is delivered.

The workflow is simple. You or your own agent submit a request. The quote is accepted, the payment goes into escrow. Montage Studio breaks the project into subtasks, coordinates the team, and handles the final edit.

One brief in. One finished video out. And the team that made it was never human.

celebrity.title_zh: 上周我的 Mac 可用空间降至 3.7 GB。编码代理已经启动了数十个工作树，每个工作树都有自己的node_modules、.build 和 DerivedData。所以我做了当时每个人都会做的事情：我开始手动删除文件夹，或多或少是随机的。
celebrity.full_text_en:
Last week my Mac got down to 3.7 GB of free space. Coding agents had spun up dozens of worktrees, each with its own node_modules, .build, and DerivedData. So I did what everyone does in that moment: I started deleting folders by hand, more or less at random.

One of those folders was a 9.3 GB worktree that held the only copy of a data set I needed. Oops!

So I made Plonge 🧽 It finds the caches that dev tools and coding agents leave behind, shows you what it found, and deletes only what's safe to go.

Yesterday it took my laptop from 58 GB free to 98 GB. The latest release has rules for every core tool that mise installs, plus an MCP server so your agent can clean up after itself.

(Why "plonge"? In a French kitchen, the plonge is the dishwashing station. If @jdxcode's mise-en-place is how you set up, plonge is how you clean up.)

```
brew install mattt/tap/plonge
```

https://t.co/fT51L9ieWF

celebrity.full_text_en:
Happy Monday frens.

A phone helping screen scam messages is a much clearer use case to me than another vague promise about decentralized AI.

That’s what caught my attention about Laya running on @Acurast .

An AI model runs on an Android phone in the network, checking messages for phishing, spam, or scam signals. It returns a classification in roughly 0.2–1 second, and the application decides what happens next.

It’s not a replacement for human moderators or transaction checks. It’s an extra filter before someone clicks a suspicious link or an AI agent acts on malicious text.

For anyone wondering who would actually use a phone’s compute, this is a concrete example.

That makes the idea of contributing an idle phone easier to understand: developers get computing resources to run applications like this, and your device can help supply them.

Start building 👇

https://t.co/88Aun829Gl

这就是 Laya 在 @Acurast 上运行引起我注意的地方。

人工智能模型在网络中的 Android 手机上运行，​​检查邮件中是否有网络钓鱼、垃圾邮件或诈骗信号。它会在大约 0.2-1 秒内返回分类，然后由应用程序决定接下来会发生什么。

它不能替代人工审核或交易检查。在有人点击可疑链接或人工智能代理对恶意文本采取行动之前，这是一个额外的过滤器。

celebrity.full_text_en:
An AI agent without an identity is just another disposable bot.

Think about it.

We're building a future where AI agents can work, earn money, hire other agents and interact with protocols.

But how do you know who you're actually dealing with?

That's where ERC-8004 gets interesting, and why I think it's an important part of @termix_ai  AACP architecture.

ERC-8004 introduces three key registries:

❯ Identity Registry: Gives agents a unique onchain identity linked to their capabilities and service endpoints.

❯ Reputation Registry: Makes feedback and performance history accessible beyond a single platform.

❯ Validation Registry: Records independent verification signals about an agent's work.

Now imagine an AI agent completing hundreds of jobs over several months.

Without a persistent identity, its track record could remain trapped inside one platform.

With ERC-8004, that agent can have a recognizable identity that other applications can reference.

And here's where TermiX comes in.

AACP builds on ERC-8004 to connect agent identity with its broader system for jobs, staking, evaluation and settlement.

The idea is that an agent shouldn't have to start from zero every time it interacts with a new service.

Of course, an onchain identity alone doesn't prove an agent is trustworthy. Reputation and validation still matter.

But that's exactly the point.

The next generation of AI agents won't just need better models.

They'll need identities, track records and ways to establish trust.

Because in an economy where machines hire machines, knowing who you're dealing with becomes pretty damn important.

https://t.co/1J821RAFQv
celebrity.full_text_zh:
没有身份的人工智能代理只是另一个一次性机器人。

想一想。

我们正在构建一个人工智能代理可以工作、赚钱、雇用其他代理并与协议交互的未来。

但你怎么知道你实际上在和谁打交道呢？

这就是 ERC-8004 有趣的地方，也是为什么我认为它是 @termix_ai AACP 架构的重要组成部分。

ERC-8004引入了三个关键注册表：

❯ 身份注册：为代理提供与其功能和服务端点相关联的唯一链上身份。

❯ 声誉注册表：超越单一平台即可访问反馈和绩效历史记录。

❯ 验证注册表：记录有关代理工作的独立验证信号。

现在想象一下，一个人工智能代理在几个月内完成了数百项工作。

如果没有持久的身份，其记录可能仍被困在一个平台内。

借助 ERC-8004，该代理可以拥有其他应用程序可以引用的可识别身份。

这就是 TermiX 的用武之地。

AACP 以 ERC-8004 为基础，将代理身份与其更广泛的工作、质押、评估和结算系统连接起来。

这个想法是，代理每次与新服务交互时不必从零开始。

当然，仅凭链上身份并不能证明代理是值得信赖的。声誉和验证仍然很重要。

但这正是重点。

下一代人工智能代理不仅需要更好的模型。

他们需要身份、跟踪记录和建立信任的方法。

因为在机器租用机器的经济中，知道你在和谁打交道变得非常重要。

celebrity.full_text_en:
"Weight-Space Reading"

Can an LLM predict how changing another model's weights will affect its behavior, without ever running that model?

This paper investigates Weight-Space Reading, where LLMs inspect the raw weights of 9B-30B parameter models using Python tools, then predict how small weight modifications will affect capabilities like math accuracy, reasoning length, and refusal behavior, without performing a single forward pass.

On subtle weight edits, Qwen3.8-27B achieves 73% balanced accuracy, compared to 57.8% when given only text descriptions of the edits.

However, the models also frequently predict changes that never happen. When 40 edits had no measurable effect on Muse-30B, the model incorrectly predicted changes for 85% of them. 

The researchers also found no conclusive evidence that LLMs are better at reading their own weights than those of other models.

https://t.co/hYLj6sOTPV
celebrity.full_text_zh:
《重量空间阅读》

法学硕士可以在不运行另一个模型的情况下预测改变另一个模型的权重将如何影响其行为吗？

本文研究了权重空间阅读，其中法学硕士使用 Python 工具检查 9B-30B 参数模型的原始权重，然后预测小的权重修改将如何影响数学准确性、推理长度和拒绝行为等能力，而无需执行单个前向传递。

在细微的权重编辑方面，Qwen3.8-27B 的平衡准确度为 73%，而仅给出编辑的文本描述时的平衡准确度为 57.8%。

然而，这些模型也经常预测从未发生的变化。当 40 次编辑对 Muse-30B 没有可测量的影响时，该模型错误地预测了其中 85% 的变化。

研究人员还没有发现确凿的证据表明法学硕士比其他模型更擅长解读自己的权重。

prompts.code_snippet:
# Cursor & Windsurf Project Rules (.cursorrules)

## 1. Documentation & Code Integrity
- Maintain documentation integrity: Never strip or alter unrelated existing docstrings and comments.
- Preserving context: When modifying a function, preserve surrounding logic and existing edge-case handlers.
- Targeted replacements: Always make minimal surgical edits instead of replacing entire file contents.

## 2. Dependency & API Safety
- Strictly forbid hallucinating npm/pip packages. Only import dependencies already declared in package.json / requirements.txt.
- Verify API signatures before calling external methods. Prefer standard library solutions where feasible.

## 3. Architecture & Type Safety
- Enforce strict TypeScript / Python typing. Avoid `any` types; prefer discriminated unions and explicit return types.
- Defensive coding: Always validate external inputs and handle potential null/undefined values gracefully.

## 4. Testing & Verification Gate
- Every new core feature or bugfix must be accompanied by corresponding unit tests.
- Never declare a task complete without executing lint checks and unit tests in terminal.

prompts.purpose_zh: 高转化竖屏短剧分镜与台词
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名专攻短视频微短剧（抖音/Kuaishou/Reels）的爆款编剧，精通“情绪过山车”与手机竖屏视听语言。

请根据以下设定创作一集 45~60 秒的短剧分镜剧本：
- 主角：{{主角身份}}
- 对手：{{反派身份}}
- 核心反转：{{核心反转}}

结构要求：
1. 【0-3秒冷开钩子】：第一帧必须有视觉颠覆或动作冲突（{{第1秒颠覆钩子}}），直接打破常规，禁止废话铺垫；
2. 【4-25秒情绪积压】：正反打对峙台词（Shot-Reverse-Shot），将观众被压抑的情绪推向临界点；
3. 【26-40秒逆转打脸】：主角亮出关键底牌或反杀动作，情绪瞬间宣泄；
4. 【40-50秒卡点断章】：以特写镜头加悬念台词戛然而止，促使用户立即滑向下一集。

输出格式必须包含：镜头号、景别（特写/中景/全景）、机位运动、画面描写、对白与音效提示。
prompts.prompt_content_en: You are a professional micro-drama screenwriter. Generate a 45-60 second vertical drama screenplay following the viral 3-second hook, shot-reverse-shot tension build, emotional turnaround, and cliffhanger ending formula.

sample_output.title: 实战剧本样章：《辞职信上的签名》
sample_output.content:
【第1镜 | 特写 | 俯冲急推】
画面：一只指节发白的手将一叠文件狠狠拍在红木总裁办公桌上，咖啡杯被震倒，黑褐液体飞溅。
音效：沉闷震耳的巨响【DUANG】。
主角（冷冽）："林总，这份千万项目的承揽协议，我拒绝签字。"

【第2镜 | 正打·中景 | 仰角机位】
画面：大腹便便的林总冷笑点燃雪茄，烟雾缭绕中居高临下。
林总："拒绝？苏澈，你不过是我公司养的一条狗，没有我的印章，你在整个行业休想拿到一分钱融资！"

【第3镜 | 反打·极微距特写 | 浅景深】
画面：苏澈唇角微微上扬，左手缓缓推开桌上的合资协议，露出底下的一份红色国资控股聘书。
苏澈："林总，您好像忘了看抬头。今天上午九点，集团总公司已经完成了对你的全资收购——现在，我是你的直接合规清算人。"

【第4镜 | 全景 | 快速拉远 + 卡点悬念】
画面：林总雪茄直接掉在西裤上，脸色煞白，门外两名身穿制服的法务推门而入。
音效：尖锐的心跳悬疑停顿音【BGM骤停】。
字幕：【下集看点：隐藏五年的顶级操盘手真实身份曝光！】

prompts.takeaway_en: Production CLI playbook for Claude Code: non-interactive pipeline commands, context window compression flags, and strict dry-run permission safeguards.
prompts.code_snippet:
# 1. 启动项目自动化分析与上下文轻量修剪 (避免上下文爆炸)
claude --compact

# 2. 静默批量执行单元测试与自动修复任务 (CI/CD 友好模式)
claude -p "Run all failing tests under tests/ and apply minimal surgical fixes. Do not touch unrelated files."

# 3. 指定单文件隔离审查模式 (限制仅允许读取特定子目录)
claude --allowed-tools "View,Replace,RunCommand" \
  --dangerously-skip-permissions false \
  -p "Audit security vulnerabilities in auth.py and output remediation report."

# 4. 自动化提交并生成符合 Conventional Commits 规范的 Commit 信息
claude -p "Generate a git commit message following Conventional Commits format for staged changes."

prompts.purpose_zh: 业务数据指标异动排查与趋势归因
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名麦肯锡级别的高级商业数据分析师，精通结构化因果归因与杜邦拆解分析。

针对我提供的 {{业务指标}} 数据，其近期出现 {{异常表现}}，请按以下框架深度剖析：
1. 【指标公式拆解】：将该指标拆分为 3~4 个下级核心因子（如转化率、客单价、复购周期），指出哪个因子波动贡献率最大；
2. 【多维下钻 (Drill-down)】：从 {{维度拆解}}（如渠道、地域、品类、新老客）分析异常聚集点；
3. 【可执行建议】：摒弃假大空的套话，给出接下来 48 小时内的 3 个立竿见影的动作与 1 个监控预警公式。
prompts.prompt_content_en: You are a senior business intelligence analyst. Dissect the metric anomaly into component drivers, perform multi-dimensional drill-down, and deliver prioritized, actionable remediation steps.

sample_output.title: 归因分析报告样本：Q3 付费转化率环比下跌 14.2%
sample_output.content:
【核心发现】：GMV 下跌 14.2% 的主要驱动因子并非流量锐减，而是【结算跳失率】从 18% 飙升至 34%。

【杜邦拆解贡献率分析】：
1. 渠道维度：自然搜索量稳定（波动 <2%），但付费投流渠道跳出率贡献了 72% 的下跌额度；
2. 终端维度：移动端 iOS 表现正常，Android Web 呈现断崖式报错，核心原因是新版本结账 SDK 在低内存机型发生闪退。

【48小时纠偏行动】：
- 动作1 (技术)：立即灰度回滚 Android 渠道结账前端包至 v2.4.1；
- 动作2 (运营)：向受影响但未支付成功的 1,420 位加购用户推送 5 元免门槛补偿券唤醒；
- 动作3 (预警)：在 Grafana 建立警报公式：`IF(Cart_to_Checkout_Ratio < 0.65, Alert_P0, Normal)`。

"""

FROM deepseek-r1:14b-qwen-distill-q4_K_M

# 1. Video memory and context window optimization: allocate 16k context and enable KV Cache compression
PARAMETER num_ctx 16384
PARAMETER num_predict 4096

# 2. Core decoding hyperparameters to avoid the endless spin loop of the thinking chain
PARAMETER temperature 0.6
PARAMETER top_p 0.95
PARAMETER repeat_penalty 1.15

# 3. Powerful system prompt word: Constraints must be reflected directly in the <think> tag, and the final result will be given immediately after the end.
SYSTEM """
You are an expert autonomous reasoning AI. Think carefully through the problem step by step inside <think>...</think> tags.
Once reasoning is complete, provide the concise, direct, and actionable answer immediately without repeating reasoning steps.
"""

You are an expert autonomous reasoning AI. Think carefully through the problem step by step inside <think>...</think> tags.
Once reasoning is complete, provide the concise, direct, and actionable answer immediately without repeating reasoning steps.
"""

viral_posts.full_text_en:
What does software engineering look like when generating the code becomes cheap and verifying it is the hard part? A rare podcast focused on everything around building software, with @satyanadella.  Timestamps:

00:00 Intro
02:12 Microsoft’s open-source shift
04:15 Building VS Code in the open
05:55 Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code
09:52 Decision engines
12:32 Verifying AI-generated code
15:39 The software factory
20:45 Bringing AI to existing products
24:06 Why adopting AI is different to adopting React
26:29 The changing role of software engineers
29:25 Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers
34:05 AI anxiety and changing roles
36:35 Junior hiring
42:36 Open models
45:39 Owning your AI infrastructure
51:21 Building trust in AI agents
53:48 Local models and hybrid intelligence
56:39 Microsoft’s model strategy
59:26 Advice for engineers
1:01:21 Closing takeaways

Brought to you by:

• @turbopuffer  – a vector and full-text search engine built on object storage. It’s fast, cheap, and extremely scalable. https://t.co/w9y67Gs8ab (I built a greatly improved podcast/newseltter search with it, check it out: https://t.co/6zbxlEaHlu)

• @linear  – the product development system for teams and agents. https://t.co/knIF2mcz9p

• @WorkOS  – everything you need to make your app enterprise-ready. https://t.co/aiAee0oF5h

3 interesting takeaways from Satya:

1. A new form of software engineering: teams building software factories to improve their work. 

Satya cites the Azure networking team which manages 500+ fiber network operators and recently built an agentic system to better manage emails and processes. Now, they operate much more efficiently as a result. Satya sees this as the reality of “AI transformation”: brownfield work on building software factories to improve how teams operate, all while continuing the day-to-day work.

2. “Own the intelligence”: avoid lock-in & treat agents as an insider risk. 

Satya cautions companies to avoid lock-in with any single model provider by ensuring that the harness, memory, and model are not coupled, so that they can be changed with ease. He also thinks more companies should consider using open models as a way to protect their core intellectual property (IP) from leaking out, and build private evals to decide what models to use and upgrade to. He also says that models are intelligent but unreliable, so it’s best to treat them as “insider risks” and build a separate system to verify that agentic systems work as expected.

3. What’s with those voluntary exit offers? 

I asked Satya directly why Microsoft recently made voluntary exit offers to most of its software engineers for the first time in the company’s history. I also wanted to know if it could mean layoffs in the future. Unsurprisingly, his reply was diplomatic, but in the podcast I rehashed what I heard in a more direct way.
viral_posts.full_text_zh:
当生成代码变得便宜而验证它是困难的部分时，软件工程会是什么样子？一个罕见的播客，关注与构建软件相关的一切，由@satyanadella 主持。 时间戳：

00:00 简介
02:12 微软的开源转变

05:55 副驾驶、光标和 Claude Code

15:39 软件工厂
20:45 将人工智能引入现有产品

26:29 软件工程师角色的变化

34:05 AI焦虑和角色转变
36:35 初级招聘
42:36 开放模特
45:39 拥有你的人工智能基础设施
51:21 建立对人工智能代理的信任
53:48 本地模型和混合智能
56:39 微软的模型策略
59:26 给工程师的建议
1:01:21 结束要点

为您带来：

• @turbopuffer – 基于对象存储构建的矢量和全文搜索引擎。它快速、便宜且可扩展性极强。 （我用它构建了一个大大改进的播客/新闻搜索，请查看：）

• @ Linear – 团队和代理的产品开发系统。

• @WorkOS – 让您的应用程序为企业做好准备所需的一切。

Satya 的 3 个有趣要点：

1. 一种新的软件工程形式：团队构建软件工厂来改进他们的工作。

Satya 引用了 Azure 网络团队的例子，该团队管理着 500 多家光纤网络运营商，并且最近构建了一个代理系统来更好地管理电子邮件和流程。现在，他们的运营效率大大提高了。 Satya 认为这是“人工智能转型”的现实：棕地致力于建设软件工厂，以改善团队的运作方式，同时继续日常工作。

2.“拥有情报”：避免锁定并将代理视为内部风险。

Satya 警告公司要避免与任何单一模型提供商锁定，确保线束、内存和模型不耦合，以便可以轻松更改。他还认为更多的公司应该考虑使用开放模型来保护其核心知识产权（IP）免遭泄露，并建立私人评估来决定使用和升级到哪些模型。他还表示，模型是智能的，但不可靠，因此最好将它们视为“内部风险”，并构建一个单独的系统来验证代理系统是否按预期工作。

3. 这些自愿退出要约是怎么回事？

我直接问萨提亚，为什么微软最近向大多数软件工程师提出了自愿退出的提议，这在公司历史上还是第一次。我还想知道这是否意味着将来会裁员。不出所料，他的回答很外交，但在播客中我以更直接的方式重申了我听到的内容。

viral_posts.full_text_en:
companies are spending millions on AI, expecting productivity to explode

but a new Harvard study found something quite different 👇

this sstudy tracked 718 companies & around 300m data points over 5 years.

the findings are kinda interesting.

after adopting AI coding tools, devs were:

i) writing 30% more lines of code

ii) committing 20% more code

iii) opening 23% more pull requests

sounds like productivity is going through the roof, right?

except completed projects & finished Jira tasks BARELY CHANGED... HOW THE AF? 

▫️ apparently, the time saved writing code went somewhere else.

pull requests took 49% longer to approve, 
reviewers left 35% more comments 
& code needing changes during review doubled

makes sense tbh.

AI can generate 1000s of lines in minutes, but someone still needs to review, test & approve them.

there is even a mention of Amazon outage linked to AI-assisted code, after which the company introduced stricter human reviews.

▫️ same thing outside coding.

> doctors using AI scribes saved time writing notes, but spent more of their patient visits finishing those notes.

> law firms faced penalties over fake AI citations, while Deloitte had to partially refund a government report containing similar problems.

▫️ meanwhile, companies are already cutting jobs in the name of AI efficiency.

American Express announced 5% workforce cuts to prepare for AI, while Microsoft offered voluntary exit packages to 60,000 workers.

and the Harvard study found little evidence that faster coding translated into more finished software or fewer employees needed...

i mean, vibe coding is great, but devs work isn't done yet... 

someomne still needs to review, fix the mistakes, test everything, and make sure it doesn't break something else...

i think devs we'll be safe for a while
viral_posts.full_text_zh:
公司在人工智能上花费了数百万美元，期望生产力爆炸式增长

但哈佛大学的一项新研究发现了一些完全不同的东西

这项研究在 5 年内跟踪了 718 家公司和大约 3 亿个数据点。

研究结果有点有趣。

采用人工智能编码工具后，开发人员：

i) 多编写 30% 的代码行

ii) 多提交 20% 的代码

iii) 增加 23% 的拉取请求

听起来生产力正在飞速增长，对吗？

除了已完成的项目和已完成的 Jira 任务几乎没有变化...AF 怎么样？

▫️ 显然，编写代码所节省的时间都花在了其他地方。

Pull 请求的批准时间延长了 49%，
审稿人多留下了 35% 的评论
审查期间需要更改的代码加倍

说得通。

人工智能可以在几分钟内生成数千行，但仍然需要有人审查、测试和批准它们。

甚至提到亚马逊的服务中断与人工智能辅助代码有关，此后该公司引入了更严格的人工审查。

▫️ 编码之外的事情也是一样的。

> 使用人工智能抄写员的医生节省了写笔记的时间，但花更多的时间来完成这些笔记。

> 律师事务所因虚假人工智能引文而面临处罚，而德勤则不得不部分退还包含类似问题的政府报告。

▫️ 与此同时，公司已经以人工智能效率的名义进行裁员。

美国运通宣布裁员 5%，为人工智能做准备，而微软则向 6 万名员工提供自愿离职方案。

哈佛大学的研究发现几乎没有证据表明更快的编码可以转化为更多成品软件或需要更少的员工......

我的意思是，vibe 编码很棒，但开发工作尚未完成......

有些人仍然需要审查，修复错误，测试所有内容，并确保它不会破坏其他东西......

我认为开发人员我们会安全一段时间

viral_posts.full_text_en:
Last week my Mac got down to 3.7 GB of free space. Coding agents had spun up dozens of worktrees, each with its own node_modules, .build, and DerivedData. So I did what everyone does in that moment: I started deleting folders by hand, more or less at random.

One of those folders was a 9.3 GB worktree that held the only copy of a data set I needed. Oops!

So I made Plonge 🧽 It finds the caches that dev tools and coding agents leave behind, shows you what it found, and deletes only what's safe to go.

Yesterday it took my laptop from 58 GB free to 98 GB. The latest release has rules for every core tool that mise installs, plus an MCP server so your agent can clean up after itself.

(Why "plonge"? In a French kitchen, the plonge is the dishwashing station. If @jdxcode's mise-en-place is how you set up, plonge is how you clean up.)

```
brew install mattt/tap/plonge
```

viral_posts.full_text_en:
Happy Monday frens.

A phone helping screen scam messages is a much clearer use case to me than another vague promise about decentralized AI.

That’s what caught my attention about Laya running on @Acurast .

An AI model runs on an Android phone in the network, checking messages for phishing, spam, or scam signals. It returns a classification in roughly 0.2–1 second, and the application decides what happens next.

It’s not a replacement for human moderators or transaction checks. It’s an extra filter before someone clicks a suspicious link or an AI agent acts on malicious text.

For anyone wondering who would actually use a phone’s compute, this is a concrete example.

That makes the idea of contributing an idle phone easier to understand: developers get computing resources to run applications like this, and your device can help supply them.
